_readme: roadmap: the beginner path shown as numbered steps. platforms: practice sites (those with a slug get their own page under /resources). platformPages: the text on the Kattis, Codeforces and LeetCode pages. books: reading material. The problems on each platform page come from Admin → Problems, grouped by the link's site.

roadmap.title: Pick a language and learn input/output
roadmap.text: Use C++ or Python (Java works too). Learn how to read input from standard input and print output, because every judge works this way. Grab a starter template below.

roadmap.title: Solve 20 easy problems
roadmap.text: Loops, conditionals, arrays and strings. Don't worry about speed yet. The goal is getting comfortable turning a problem statement into working code.

roadmap.title: Learn complexity (Big-O)
roadmap.text: Learn to estimate whether your solution will run in time. Roughly 10⁸ simple operations per second is a good rule of thumb.

roadmap.title: Core techniques
roadmap.text: Sorting, binary search, prefix sums, greedy, recursion and brute force. Then graphs (BFS, DFS, shortest paths) and dynamic programming.

roadmap.title: Compete regularly
roadmap.text: Join club contests and Codeforces rounds. Timed contests train speed and nerves, and upsolving the problems you missed afterwards is where most learning happens.

roadmap.title: Train as a team for ICPC
roadmap.text: ICPC is three people sharing one computer. Practise splitting problems, pair-debugging, and building a team reference document (notebook). The regional is judged with PC², so get used to submitting through it in practice rounds.

platforms.name: Kattis
platforms.text: Thousands of problems rated by difficulty, including many from past ICPC contests. We use it for club practice and contests.

platforms.name: Codeforces
platforms.text: Rated contests several times a week, plus a huge problem archive with tags. The best place to track your progress.

platforms.name: LeetCode
platforms.text: Interview-style problems. Great for co-op and internship prep, and a gentle introduction to data structures.

platforms.name: CSES Problem Set
platforms.text: 300 classic problems that pair with the CSES Handbook. Work through it topic by topic.

books.name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook
books.author: Antti Laaksonen (CSES)
books.text: Free PDF. A clear, compact tour of almost everything you need for ICPC regionals. Start here.

books.name: USACO Guide
books.author: USACO community
books.text: Free, structured modules from Bronze to Platinum with problems for every topic.

books.name: cp-algorithms
books.author: Community
books.text: Reference articles with code for almost every standard algorithm and data structure.

kattis.name: Kattis
kattis.intro: Kattis is where our club contests run. It has thousands of problems, including many from past ICPC contests, each with a difficulty score.
tips: Your program reads the input from standard input and prints the answer to standard output. Use one of our starter templates.
Submit by uploading your file. You get a verdict in seconds: Accepted, Wrong Answer, Time Limit Exceeded or Run Time Error.
Each problem has a difficulty score. Start with the lowest ones and move up.

codeforces.name: Codeforces
codeforces.intro: Codeforces runs rated contests several times a week and has a huge problem archive. Every problem has a rating, so it's easy to pick the right level.
tips: Problem ratings start at 800. Solve 800s comfortably before moving up by about 100 at a time.
Div. 3 and Div. 4 contests are aimed at newer contestants. Join one live, then upsolve the problems you didn't finish.
Like Kattis, your program reads standard input and prints to standard output.

leetcode.name: LeetCode
leetcode.intro: LeetCode is the go-to site for technical interview prep. Problems are labelled Easy, Medium and Hard and are grouped by topic.
tips: Unlike Kattis and Codeforces, you write a function, not a full program: there's no input to read yourself.
Practise explaining your approach out loud, as you would in an interview.
Once a problem passes, look at its time and space complexity and see whether you can do better.
